4. The suit was decreed on contest. On appeal the High. Court Division reversed some of the findings of the trial court and modified the decree in part. 

 5. Being aggrieved, plaintiff-appellant moved this Court and obtained leave to consider whether the learned Judges acted correctly in modifying the decree passed by the trial court without reversing the finding of the trial court on this question and whether the learned Judges were correct in placing the onus upon the plaintiff to prove that 3337 bags of cement were not wrongly covered by the Short Landing Certificate and. the same also were not lying in Shed No. 5 in damaged condition, although the plaintiff's witnesses categorically denied the suggestion that 3337 bags of cement were still lying after 9300 bags were cleared ; and the defendants' witnesses also could not prove that 3337 bags of cement in damaged condition were lying in shed No. 5. 

 6. The contention as to whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division were correct in modifying the decree of the trial court without finding as to whether it was wrong in its conclusions on the relevant fact as to the short landing and the conduct of the plaintiff as appeared from its witnesses relate to the short delivery of 3337 bags of cement. Facts involved in the case, as already seen, arc short. Out of the total quantity of cement imported 79025 bags of cement were allotted to the plaintiff-Railway which submitted bill of entry when the Chartered Ship S.S. Floram berthed at Chittagong Port and discharged its cargo. Plaintiff-appellant got delivery of 73458 bags of cement thus showing that 5567 bags were not delivered. Consequently, plaintiff-appellant applied for issuing short landing certificate which was issued on November 16, 1964, vide Ext. 7. It showed that 5567 bags were landed short from the ship. Plaintiff thereupon sent its letter of claim, Ext. 5 and submitted the claim bill Ext. 5(a). Plain-tiff-appellant also served a notice under section 9 of the Ports Act upon the Port Authority, defendant No. 4. 

 9. The trial court, therefore, found that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were jointly liable for the loss of 5567 bags of cement. Its further conclusion was that defendant No. 4, the Port Authority, had no liability since it issued the short landing certificate in respect of the aforesaid quantity of bags and as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 could not show as to how defendant No.4 could be made liable for the same. On hearing the appeal against the trial court's decree by the defendant No. 1 the learned Judges of the High Court Division arrived at some different conclusions regarding the quantity of cement short landed. in making conclusions the learned Judges considered Ext. B(1) which is the out-turn report of the vessel issued by the Port Authority. This exhibit shows that 5567 bags of cement were short landed. At the same time it shows that 3337 bags of cement out of the aforesaid quantity were delivered in damaged condition and stored in shed No. 5. Though Ext. 7 which is the short landing certificate recorded that 5567 bags were landed short, it made no reference that 3337 bags were landed in damaged condition. The natural deductions from a consideration of these two documents would be that unless it could be established by the Port Authority that the fact of storage of 3337 bags in shed No. 5 was brought to the notice of the plaintiff-appellant, it cannot escape liability regarding the same. There is no evidence to show that while issuing the short landing certificate in respect of 5567 bags the Port Authority mentioned about the storage of 3337 bags of cement in shed No. 5, nor has it tried to prove that this fact was brought to the notice of the plaintiff-appellant. Under these circumstances it cannot be held that the plaintiff-appellant was responsible for not taking delivery of 3337 bags of cement. The position, of course, would have been different had the plaintiff-appellant any knowledge of the storage of the aforesaid quantity of cement in shed No. 5. Nowhere in the evidence has this knowledge been attributed to the plaintiff or proved against it. 

 10. From a mere consideration of the out-turn report, namely, Ext. B(I), which shows that 3337 bags were landed in damaged condition and were stored in shed No. 5 the learned Judges of the High Court division came to conclude that this quantity of bags must be deducted from 5567 bags and the quantity of bags actually short landed should come down to 2230 bags only. Plaintiff-appellant was, therefore, decreed the proportionate value of 2230 bags and its claim with regard to 3337 bags of cement was accordingly dismissed. As to not taking delivery of 3337 bags of cement which, as appears from the out-turn report, were landed in damaged condition and stored in shed No. 5 the learned Judges arrived at the following finding: 

 15. In the facts and circumstances of the case and upon consideration of the evidence, there appears no justification for modifying the trial courts decree as done by the High Court Division. It also appears that its conclusion regarding the liability as to 1337 bags is not justified. The Port Authority must be held responsible for the same. The distinction between short landing and landing in damaged condition is clear enough and as such by its omission to notify the plaintiff-appellant regarding the delivery of 3337 bags of cement in damaged condition and storage in shed No. 5, it deprived the plaintiff-appellant the chance either to apply for survey or take delivery of the aforesaid quantity in damaged condition. There is also no evidence as to what happened to 3337 bags of cement alleged to have been stored in shed No. 5. 

 16. The question that remains to be determined is whether the decree can be passed jointly against defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 or in the alternative, whether plaintiff-appellant should be directed to file a separate suit claiming compensation for the non-delivery of 3337 bags of cement against the defendant No. 4 and the decree should be passed for only 2230 bags of cement short landed. 1 do not had that there is necessity for filing a separate suit claiming the value of 3337 bags of cement from the Port Authority. Facts as established in the case by evidence on record, show clearly that the entire quantity of bags which is the subject matter of the claim, namely, 5567 bags of cement were covered by the short landing certificate, Ext. 7, and there being no mention anywhere that out of the said quantity, 3337 bags of cement were landed in damaged condition and stored in shed No. 5. When the letter of claim was sent by the plaintiff-appellant and defendant No 4, Port Authority, issued a short landing certificate it ought to have taken care to mention about the delivery of 3337 bags of cement in damaged condition and that they were stored in shed No. 5 so as to absolve itself from its liability. Responsibility to issue the short landing certificate is entirely of the Port Authority and the plaintiff-appellant has no share in it. It may also be mentioned that defendant No. 4 did not even file any written statement making its position clear in respect of delivery of 3337 bags of cement in damaged condition. It is too late in the day to prove that it is not liable in any way.
